ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaling of tour error with city count for a fixed-capacity solver
PROPOSAL: Train a graph transformer with six layers and embedding width 256 on Euclidean tours over uniform points in the unit square. Raise the city count through 20, 40, 80, 160 and 320 while the architecture stays unchanged, and supervise with optimal tours from an exact branch-and-cut solver. Train each model on a stream of fresh instances until validation tour length stops improving, so the model, not the data, sets the limit. Fit a saturating power law to the optimality gap against the logarithm of the number of possible tours.
CONTROLS: Nearest-neighbour and farthest-insertion tours on the same test instances, three training seeds per city count, a smaller model with half the width to confirm that the gap responds to capacity, and a check that the validation loss is flat at the end of every run.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: The gap should rise smoothly and close to a power law in the log of the tour count, with the fitted exponent stable across seeds. The fit fails if the larger city counts bend away from the trend or if seed spread exceeds the change between neighbouring counts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Curse of dimensionality for routing networks on Euclidean tours
PROPOSAL: Hold the number of cities at 50 and place the points uniformly in a unit cube whose dimension rises from 2 through 3, 4, 6 and 10. Train a transformer with a fixed count of 4 million parameters on a stream of fresh instances, taking targets from an exact solver in low dimension and from a long local-search run in the highest ones. Record the optimality gap on 2500 test instances per dimension once validation tour length has settled, then fit gap against dimension with both a power law and an exponential form.
CONTROLS: The comparison runs against nearest-neighbour tours in each dimension, against the same network trained on 25 cities to see which part of the loss comes from dimension rather than city count, and against three training seeds per dimension so that spread is known before any trend is read.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: The gap should climb with dimension and slow down once distances between points concentrate. The trend would be in doubt if the exponential and power forms fit equally badly or if the highest dimensions show a gap below that of the middle ones.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modelling the capacity limit of a routing network on tours
PROPOSAL: Hold the problem at 100 cities and train routing transformers whose embedding width is 64, 128, 256 and 512, each on an endless supply of fresh uniform instances until validation tour length stops moving. Optimise with the same schedule for every width and take targets from an exact solver. Fit a saturating curve of optimality gap against parameter count and report the asymptote with a confidence interval from resampled test instances. The behaviour near the asymptote is the quantity of interest, so the largest width is trained for twice as many updates as the others.
CONTROLS: The gap of every width is compared with a nearest-neighbour tour and a two-opt tour on the same 3000 test instances. Each width is repeated with three seeds, and a held-out width of 384 checks that the fitted curve generalises to a model that was not used in the fit.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: The gap should shrink with width and flatten at an asymptote clearly above zero, since a fixed network cannot encode every neighbourhood configuration. The curve fails to support this reading if the largest width keeps improving at the same rate as the smaller ones.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reinforcement learning against imitation at the capacity limit
PROPOSAL: Train two copies of one graph neural network (GNN) on Euclidean traveling salesman problem (TSP) instances with 100 cities. One copy imitates optimal tours from an exact solver, and the other uses policy-gradient reinforcement learning (RL) with negative tour length as reward. Both receive the same parameter count and the same number of fresh instances, and both are trained until validation tour length settles. Compare the settled optimality gap at 50, 100 and 200 cities and fit the dependence of the gap on city count for each method separately.
CONTROLS: Nearest-neighbour tours and two-opt tours provide the heuristic references. An RL run with a longer schedule tests whether the RL gap is still falling when training stops. Three seeds per method and city count give the spread, and one extra GNN with twice the width shows whether the limit is capacity at all.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: Imitation should reach a lower settled gap at the smaller counts, and the difference should narrow as the city count grows. The comparison would be inconclusive if the RL runs are still improving when stopped.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fitting on small tours and predicting large ones
PROPOSAL: Fit gap-versus-city-count curves on models trained with 10, 15, 20, 30 and 50 cities, using one transformer architecture with fixed width and exact-solver targets. Then train fresh models of the same architecture at 100, 200 and 400 cities and test the fitted curves against the measured gaps. Compare three functional forms, a power law, a logarithmic law and a stretched exponential, chosen before the large runs start. Large-scale models are trained until validation tour length stops moving so that the capacity limit, rather than data, is measured.
CONTROLS: The forms are compared by prediction error on the held-out large counts, not by fit quality on the small counts. A shuffled-label version of the small-count fit gives a reference for how good a trivial prediction is. Three seeds are used at each city count.
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: The power law or the stretched exponential should predict the large counts within a few points of gap, while the logarithmic form should drift. If every form misses the large counts by more than the seed spread, short-range trends do not carry over to far larger scales.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Counting local configurations as a mechanism for the gap
PROPOSAL: Test the idea that a fixed-capacity network can memorise only a limited set of local neighbourhood patterns, so its error grows with the number of distinct patterns a tour contains. Train transformers of one width on 30, 60 and 120 cities, label every city in the test tours by the density of its five nearest neighbours, and measure where the tour decisions go wrong. Predict the total gap from the share of high-density cities and the per-class error, and compare the prediction with the measured gap at 240 cities.
CONTROLS: A model of twice the width tests whether the error in each density class falls with capacity. A shuffled assignment of density labels shows what the density breakdown explains by chance. Three seeds are used per width.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: The share of high-density cities should account for most of the growth of the gap, and doubling the width should lower the error mainly in those classes. The mechanism is unsupported when the error is spread evenly over all density classes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Autoregressive and one-shot decoders under a fixed parameter count
PROPOSAL: We train a graph transformer with an autoregressive decoder and a second network of the same parameter count that predicts an edge-probability matrix in one pass, both on Euclidean tours with 20, 50, 100 and 200 cities. We supervise with tours from an exact solver and train until validation tour length is flat, with fresh instances at every step. We then compare the settled optimality gap of the two decoders at each city count and test whether the gap difference depends on city count.
CONTROLS: We use nearest-neighbour and two-opt tours as references, three seeds per decoder and city count, and a version of each network with half the width to see whether capacity separates the two decoders.
COST: 320
PREDICTION: We expect the one-shot decoder to fall behind as the city count grows, because its output matrix scales quadratically. We would read a constant difference across city counts as evidence that the decoder matters little.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Instance distribution and the constants of the scaling trend
PROPOSAL: Generate Euclidean tour instances with 100 cities from three point distributions: uniform in the unit square, a mixture of eight Gaussian clusters, and points on a jittered lattice. Train one transformer per distribution with identical width, depth and update count, using exact-solver tours as targets and fresh instances at every step. Fit the same saturating power law of optimality gap against model width for each distribution and compare the fitted exponent and the asymptote across distributions.
CONTROLS: Nearest-neighbour tours on each distribution give a measure of how hard the heuristic finds it. Cross-testing every network on the other two distributions shows how specific the fitted constants are. Three seeds are used per distribution and width.
COST: 2100
PREDICTION: The exponent should stay close across the three distributions while the asymptote shifts, with the lattice giving the smallest gap. The common-exponent reading is rejected if the exponents differ by more than the seed spread.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint law in city count and dimension for a capacity-limited model
PROPOSAL: Build a grid of problems with 10, 20, 40, 80 and 160 cities in unit cubes of dimension 2, 3, 5 and 8, and train one transformer of fixed width on each cell until validation tour length stops moving, using fresh instances and exact-solver or long local-search targets. Fit two models of the optimality gap across the grid, an additive form in the logarithms of both variables and a form with an interaction term. Compare them on cells held out of the fit.
CONTROLS: Nearest-neighbour tours on every cell provide a reference level. A network with twice the width on four cells shows how much of the gap capacity can remove. Three seeds per cell give the noise level against which the interaction term is judged.
COST: 4200
PREDICTION: The interaction term should be positive, so that adding dimensions hurts more when cities are many. The additive form is preferred if the held-out cells are predicted equally well without the interaction.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Smooth trends in tour length without an interpretable loss
PROPOSAL: Compare two performance measures for a capacity-limited routing network on 100-city Euclidean tours: the optimality gap of the decoded tour and the supervised training loss. Train transformers of widths 64 through 512, always on fresh instances and until validation tour length settles, and fit a power law of each measure against parameter count. Judge smoothness by the residual of the fit on a held-out width and by the spread across seeds.
CONTROLS: Seeds, three per width, give the noise level. Nearest-neighbour tours provide a reference for the gap, and a network trained with a different loss, an edge-wise cross-entropy, tests whether the trend belongs to the measure rather than to the loss.
COST: 260
PREDICTION: The gap should follow a clean power law in parameter count, while the loss should show a weaker or bent trend. The gap is not a good measure if its residuals are as large as those of the loss.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Optimality gap of capacity-limited routing networks as city count grows
PROPOSAL: Train a graph transformer with six layers and embedding width 192 on Euclidean tours over uniform points in the unit square, stepping the city count from 20 to 160 while leaving the architecture unchanged. Supervise with optimal tours from an exact solver and train until validation tour length stops moving, so data and optimization are not the limiting factor. Measure the optimality gap on 2000 fresh instances per city count.
CONTROLS: Compare each trained model against the optimal tour length from the exact solver on the same instances. Compare against a nearest-neighbour tour and a two-opt tour on those instances. Repeat training with three seeds and report the spread. Check that the validation curve is flat before any gap is read.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: The gap should rise smoothly with city count, close to a power law, and a fit on the smaller counts should extrapolate to the larger ones. The claim fails if the gap jumps irregularly or if validation tour length is still falling when training ends.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Tour length of message-passing models of constant width on growing instances
PROPOSAL: Fit an encoder-decoder network with five message-passing layers and embedding width 192 to Euclidean instances placed uniformly in the unit square, raising the number of cities from 30 to 240 with the architecture unchanged. Targets come from an exact solver, and each run goes on until the validation curve flattens, which keeps data volume from being the limit. Score every model by its optimality gap on 2000 newly drawn instances per city count.
CONTROLS: Compare each trained model against the tour that visits cities in the order listed on the same instances. Compare against the model's own first checkpoint and a model trained on 20 cities only, on those instances. Repeat training with three seeds and report the spread. Check that the validation curve is flat before any gap is read.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: The gap should climb steadily with city count, near a power law, and a fit on the lower counts should carry over to the higher ones. The claim fails if the gap moves erratically or if validation tour length is still dropping when training ends.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Capacity dependence of the achievable tour quality on fixed instances
PROPOSAL: Fix the city count at 100 and train transformer routing models whose embedding width takes the values 64, 128, 256 and 512, each on an unlimited stream of fresh uniform instances with optimal tours from an exact solver as targets. Continue each run until the validation tour length has settled, then fit a saturating power law to the settled gap against parameter count and read off the asymptote.
CONTROLS: Vary the embedding width while holding the stream, schedule and instance distribution fixed. Compare each width against the exact solver on the same 3000 test instances. Repeat every width with three seeds. Confirm the asymptote with a held-out width not used in the fit.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: A smooth decline of the gap with parameter count that levels off at a stable value supports the claim, while wide scatter across seeds or a curve that keeps dropping argues against it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training schedule dependence of the tour quality reached on fixed instances
PROPOSAL: Fix the city count at 100 and the model at one transformer with embedding width 256, and train it under 4 learning-rate shapes: constant, linear decay after 1000 warm-up steps, cosine decay after 2000 warm-up steps and step decay, each on an unlimited stream of fresh uniform instances with exact-solver tours as targets. Run every shape until the validation tour length has settled, then fit a saturating power law to the settled gap against training steps and read off the asymptote.
CONTROLS: Vary the learning-rate schedule while holding the stream, width and instance distribution fixed. Compare each schedule against the exact solver on the same 3000 test instances. Repeat every schedule with three seeds. Confirm the asymptote with a held-out schedule not used in the fit.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: A smooth decline of the gap with training steps that levels off at a stable value supports the claim, while wide scatter across seeds or a curve that keeps dropping argues against it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Limit of achievable performance for a fixed model on harder tours
PROPOSAL: Train one routing transformer with 3 million parameters on Euclidean tours, raising the city count through 25, 50, 100 and 200. Generate fresh instances for every update and let each run continue for at least ten times the number of steps at which validation tour length last moved, so that capacity is the only thing left to limit the result. Record the settled optimality gap against city count.
CONTROLS: Compare settled models against the exact solver on the same instances. Compare against an identical model given twice the updates. Vary the city count while holding the model fixed, and repeat with three seeds. Check the gap at the final checkpoint against the checkpoint before it.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: If capacity is the limit, the gap should settle at a level that depends on city count and stays put when training is extended. Continued improvement of the doubled run points to unfinished training, not capacity, as the cause.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Early-training behaviour of a routing transformer on harder tours
PROPOSAL: Train one routing transformer with 3 million parameters on a fixed pool of 20000 Euclidean instances, raising the city count through 25, 50, 100 and 200. Reuse the pool across passes and stop each run at the end of its first pass, so that the amount of data is the main thing limiting the result. Record the optimality gap after that pass against city count.
CONTROLS: Compare early models against the exact solver on the same instances. Compare against an identical model given half the updates. Vary the city count while holding the model fixed, and repeat with three seeds. Check the gap at the first checkpoint against the checkpoint after it.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: If data is the limit, the gap should reach a level that depends on city count and then move with the pool. Improvement of the doubled run points to unfinished training, not the pool, as the cause.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Degradation with coordinate dimension for a fixed-capacity solver
PROPOSAL: Place 50 cities uniformly in a unit cube of dimension 2, 3, 5 and 8 and train a transformer of one fixed width on fresh instances in each, with targets from an exact solver where feasible and from a long local-search run in the highest dimensions. Stop when validation tour length stops changing and fit the settled gap against dimension.
CONTROLS: Measure the optimality gap in tour length against the exact solver on 2000 held-out instances per dimension. Compare against a nearest-neighbour tour in the same dimension. Repeat with three seeds. Check the gap on instances drawn from a second uniform draw.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: The gap should widen with dimension at an accelerating pace. The reading is in doubt if the second draw disagrees with the first, or if the gap at dimension 8 falls below that at dimension 5.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Imitation accuracy of a fixed-capacity solver as coordinates gain dimensions
PROPOSAL: Sample 50 points from a unit cube with 2, 3, 5 or 8 axes, and for each of these cubes fit one network of fixed width, a six-layer encoder, on a stream of new draws, supplying step-by-step next-city labels from exact solutions when they can be computed and from extended local search otherwise. Halt once held-out cross-entropy stops changing, then regress the settled accuracy on the number of axes.
CONTROLS: Score the next-city accuracy against the exact-solver tour on 2000 held-out instances per dimension. Contrast it with a nearest-neighbour choice in the same dimension. Repeat with three seeds. Check the accuracy on instances taken from a second uniform draw.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: Accuracy should drop as axes are added, at an accelerating pace. The reading is in doubt if the second draw disagrees with the first, or if the accuracy at dimension 8 rises above that at dimension 5.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training method and the capacity-limited level of the tour gap
PROPOSAL: Train two copies of one graph transformer on Euclidean tours with 100 cities: one imitates optimal tours from an exact solver, the other applies policy-gradient reinforcement learning with negative tour length as reward. Give both the same parameter count and the same number of fresh instances, run both until validation tour length settles, and compare the settled gap.
CONTROLS: Compare the two training methods at matched parameter count and matched instance count. Compare each against the exact solver on the same 3000 test instances. Vary the city count over 50, 100 and 200 for both methods. Repeat every setting with three seeds.
COST: 2200
PREDICTION: A reliable difference between the methods at every city count, larger than the seed spread, shows that the limit depends on training. Overlapping spreads, or a method still improving at the end, leave the question open.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Label source and the capacity-limited level of the tour gap
PROPOSAL: Fit a pair of twin graph transformers to Euclidean tours over 100 cities, with imitation as the training signal in each. The first twin copies optimal tours computed by an exact solver, while the second copies tours returned by a local-search heuristic. Keep parameter count and number of fresh instances identical across twins, continue until validation tour length settles, and compare where each twin ends.
CONTROLS: Compare the two label sources at matched parameter count and matched instance count. Compare each against the exact solver on the same 3000 test instances. Vary the city count over 50, 100 and 200 for both sources. Repeat every setting with three seeds.
COST: 2200
PREDICTION: A reliable difference between the label sources at every city count, larger than the seed spread, shows that the limit depends on the labels. Overlapping spreads, or a source still improving at the end, leave the question open.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Independent scaling of city count and coordinate dimension
PROPOSAL: Build a grid of Euclidean tour problems with 10, 20, 40, 80 and 160 cities in unit cubes of dimension 2, 3, 5 and 8, so that the number of possible tours and the size of each city description move separately. Train one transformer of fixed width on every cell until validation tour length settles, with fresh instances and exact or long local-search targets, and fit the optimality gap as a function of both variables.
CONTROLS: Nearest-neighbour tours on every cell serve as reference. Three seeds per cell give the noise level. A network of twice the width trained on four cells shows how much of the gap capacity removes.
COST: 640
PREDICTION: The fitted surface should show the gap growing with both variables, with an interaction that makes added dimensions costlier when cities are many.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Instance distribution as the axis of difficulty for a routing network
PROPOSAL: Assemble Euclidean tour problems over 100 cities in a 2-dimensional square, with points drawn from mixtures of 1, 4, 16 and 64 Gaussian clusters at spread 0.05 and at spread 0.2, so that the character of the instances moves while city count and coordinate count stay constant. Train one 6-layer transformer per mixture until validation tour length settles, using fresh instances and exact-solver targets, then fit the optimality gap as a function of a clustering index.
CONTROLS: Nearest-neighbour tours on every distribution serve as reference. Three seeds per distribution give the noise level. A network of twice the width trained on two distributions shows how much of the gap capacity removes.
COST: 640
PREDICTION: The fitted curve should show the gap growing with the clustering index, with an irregularity for the ring-shaped set.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Capacity as the variable that sets the achievable tour quality
PROPOSAL: Train routing transformers across embedding widths from 32 to 512 on Euclidean tours of 200 cities, feeding an endless stream of new instances labelled by an exact solver and letting each model run until validation tour length settles. Fit the settled optimality gap to parameter count with a saturating power law, which exposes the limit left when capacity alone is scarce.
CONTROLS: Nearest-neighbour tours serve as reference. Three seeds per width give the noise level. A model trained for twice as many updates at the largest width checks that the limit does not come from stopping early.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: The gap should shrink with parameter count and approach an asymptote above zero.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training data volume as the variable that sets the achievable tour quality
PROPOSAL: Take a single routing transformer of embedding width 256 and expose it to training pools holding anywhere from 1000 up to 1000000 Euclidean instances of 200 cities each, labelled by an exact solver, with every run continuing until validation tour length settles. Relate the settled optimality gap to pool count by a saturating power law, which exposes the limit left when examples alone are scarce.
CONTROLS: A nearest-neighbour tour is the reference at each pool. Each pool is repeated with three seeds to give the noise level. Doubling the updates at the largest pool checks that the limit does not come from stopping early.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: Larger pools should push the gap down toward a limit above zero.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Extrapolating a fitted trend to city counts far outside its range
PROPOSAL: Fit gap-versus-city-count curves on transformers trained with 10, 15, 20, 30 and 50 cities, then train fresh models of one architecture at 100, 200 and 400 cities and test the fitted curves against their measured gaps. Compare a power law, a logarithmic law and a stretched exponential, all fixed before the large runs begin, and rank them by prediction error on the large counts.
CONTROLS: Exact-solver or long local-search targets serve every count. Three seeds per count give the noise level. A nearest-neighbour tour provides a reference at each count.
COST: 420
PREDICTION: One of the forms should predict the large counts to within the seed spread while the others drift.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Checking a fitted trend against intermediate city counts and new instances
PROPOSAL: Estimate curves relating the gap to city count from networks trained on 10, 20, 30 and 50 cities. Afterwards, train new networks of the same design on 15, 25 and 40 cities, draw a new set of test instances for each, and measure how closely the estimated curves match the realised gaps. Candidate families are a power law, a logarithmic law and a stretched exponential, chosen before the extra runs, and the ranking uses error at the in-between counts.
CONTROLS: Exact-solver targets cover every count. Each count is repeated with three seeds to measure noise. A nearest-neighbour tour serves as the reference at each count.
COST: 420
PREDICTION: One of the forms should predict the intermediate counts to within the seed spread while the others drift.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Testing a capacity-based mechanism for the shape of the gap curve
PROPOSAL: Test the idea that a network of fixed width can store only a limited set of local neighbourhood patterns. Train transformers of one width on 30, 60 and 120 cities, tag each city of the test tours by the density around it, and predict the total gap from the share of dense cities and the error within each class. Compare the prediction with the gap measured at 240 cities.
CONTROLS: Exact-solver tours give the labels. Three seeds per width give the noise level. A model of twice the width shows whether the error in each class falls with capacity.
COST: 90
PREDICTION: Dense cities should account for most of the growth of the gap, and wider models should lower the error mainly there.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Describing the shape of the gap curve with flexible families
PROPOSAL: Collect gap curves from transformers of one width trained on 30, 60, 120 and 240 cities and fit them with a power law, a logarithmic law, a stretched exponential and a smooth spline. Rank the families by held-out error over resampled test instances, and report the one that describes the curve best along with its parameters.
CONTROLS: Exact-solver tours give the labels. Three seeds per width give the noise level. A model of twice the width shows whether the chosen family keeps its shape as capacity changes.
COST: 90
PREDICTION: One family should describe the curve best, with the spline matching it only by using more parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Coordinate dimension as the source of the curse of dimensionality
PROPOSAL: Fix the city count at 60 and raise the coordinate dimension through 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12 for a transformer of one width, training on fresh instances in each dimension until validation tour length settles. Targets come from an exact solver at low dimension and a long local-search run at high dimension. Fit the settled optimality gap against dimension with a power law and an exponential.
CONTROLS: Nearest-neighbour tours in each dimension serve as reference. Three seeds per dimension give the noise level. A model of twice the width in the two highest dimensions shows whether capacity relieves the growth.
COST: 260
PREDICTION: The gap should rise with dimension and the exponential form should fit better once distances concentrate.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: City count as the source of combinatorial growth in the solution space
PROPOSAL: Keep the points in the plane and let the number of stops climb over 20, 40, 80, 160, 320 and 640, using a transformer of unchanged width that sees newly sampled instances at every count and trains until validation tour length settles. Labels come from an exact solver for the smaller counts and an extended local search for the larger ones. Relate the settled optimality gap to the number of stops by a power law and by an exponential.
CONTROLS: At every count a nearest-neighbour tour is the reference. Three seeds per count give the noise level. Doubling the width at the two largest counts shows whether capacity relieves the growth.
COST: 260
PREDICTION: The gap should rise with the number of stops, and the power form should fit better at large counts.
